steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an HCI paper on a Wizard-of-Oz study of how data analysts respond to AI assistants that give analysis planning suggestions, not just code. Cover the motivation, the research questions, the method and the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Data analysis as a series of decisions: planning vs. execution
- Problems caused by inadequate planning
- Analysis assistants: execution vs. planning assistance; LLMs as an opportunity
- Why planning assistance is hard to build
- Research questions
- Our approach: content categories, Wizard of Oz study
- Findings, design guidelines and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Data analysis = many decisions
  - tasks: data collection, wrangling, statistical modeling, inference
  - analysis planning: reason through effects of decisions using results, prior experience, domain + statistical knowledge
  - analysis execution: enact choices with correct code + appropriate tools
  - examine outcome -> repeat
- Inadequate planning
  - risk of arbitrary, ill-founded decisions
  - analysts struggle to identify/address relevant decision points
  - overfocus on low-level details (tuning hyperparameters); miss high-level considerations (alternative statistical / mental models)
  - center execution decisions on familiar workflows when other tools may fit better
  - unconsidered flexibility (+ biases) -> scientific reproducibility crisis
  - same task + dataset -> divergent conclusions
- Assistants
  - execution assistants (e.g. Copilot) suggest code/tools (Fig. 1 A)
  - planning assistance: reason about decisions (Fig. 1 B and C), articulate hypotheses + mental models, find overlooked alternatives/rationales
  - systematically considering alternatives deepens understanding of outcome variations
  - -> more principled, reliable, robust analyses
  - LLMs: coding, language, visualization generation
  - prior LLM assistants: execution only; planning unexplored (Fig. 2 bottom row)
- Why hard
  - not just feeding context into LLM: needs selective context, higher-level scaffolding, targeted prompts, sensitive triggers
  - iterative: interpret prior results, statistics, domain knowledge; execution-only assistants ignore this (Fig. 2 A and B)
  - may require backtracking to a prior choice (Fig. 1)
  - prompts hard to author; right context hard to identify (hallucinatory analyses)
  - non-linear: typing, reading, reflecting -> timing less clear than in software engineering
- RQs
  - RQ1: what types of planning assistance content?
  - RQ2: which suggestions helpful, when?
  - RQ3: impact on workflows; own ideas vs. adopting suggestions / exploring alternatives
- Approach
  - RQ1: literature review + crowd-sourced analysis study, 29 analyst teams, same dataset, same question (Sec. 3) -> categories of assistance content (Table 1)
  - RQ2/RQ3: Wizard of Oz study, 13 practicing analysts (Sec. 4) — contribution 1
  - same scenario as crowd-sourced study; wizard behind the scenes
  - JupyterLab extension; wizard (aided by LLMs) controls selection, quality, timing (Fig. 3)
- Findings / contribution 2
  - design guidelines (Sec. 6) from findings (Sec. 5): align intent + goals, varying levels of assistance, increase understanding + engagement
  - diverse planning assistance helps, but context matters
  - timing, statistical/domain background matter for helpfulness
  - goal mismatch: analyst (speed, completion) vs. planning assistance (methodical, robust)
- Closing: richer, more useful assistants -> more robust, reliable analysis

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Doing data analysis means analysts have to make a lot of decisions about different tasks, for example data collection, data wrangling, statistical modeling and inference. For each choice there is analysis planning, where the analyst reasons about what the potential decisions will do by putting together their results, their prior experiences, and their domain and statistical knowledge. When the decisions are made, the focus moves to actually carrying out the choices with the right code and the right software tools, and we call this analysis execution. Then the analyst looks at the outcome of the execution and the process repeats again.

When analysis planning is inadequate this flow can get complicated, and analysts risk making arbitrary and ill-founded decisions, for lots of reasons. Analysts often have a hard time identifying and addressing the decision points that are relevant. They can focus too much on low-level details like tuning hyperparameters, or they miss high-level considerations such as alternative statistical or mental models. Often they center their execution decisions on workflows they are familiar with, even when approaches with other tools might be more applicable. Also, the flexibility in decision-making that nobody considers (and the biases that come with it) contributes to the reproducibility crisis in science. For example, when analysts get the same analysis task and the same dataset they often come to divergent conclusions.

Data analysis assistants try to bridge these gaps by helping analysts to execute and plan their analyses. Execution assistants based on AI (for example Copilot) help analysts implement their decisions (Fig. 1 A) by suggesting code or tools. Planning assistance is different, it may help analysts reason about their decisions (Fig. 1 B and C), articulate their hypotheses and mental models, and identify alternative decisions or rationales that they overlooked (Fig. 1). Considering alternatives systematically can deepen how well analysts understand the outcome variations that are latent to decision-making in data analysis. So planning assistance can be a transformative step towards analyses that are more principled, reliable and robust.

Large language models (LLMs) have improved capabilities for coding, language and generating visualizations, and this gives an opportunity to make planning and execution data analysis assistants a reality. Previous LLM-based assistants explored practical approaches for execution assistance, but planning is still unexplored (Fig. 2 bottom row).

- Why planning assistance is hard
  - not just feeding context into LLM: selective context, higher-level scaffolding, targeted prompts, sensitive triggers
  - iterative interpretation of prior results, statistics, domain knowledge; execution-only assistants ignore it (Fig. 2 A and B)
  - backtracking to prior choice (Fig. 1)
  - prompts hard to author; right context hard to find (hallucinatory analyses)
  - non-linear -> suggestion timing less clear than in software engineering
- RQs
  - RQ1 types of planning assistance content
  - RQ2 helpful suggestions and when
  - RQ3 impact on workflows; own ideas vs. adopting suggestions
- Approach
  - literature review + crowd-sourced study (29 analyst teams, same dataset/question, Sec. 3) -> content categories (Table 1)
  - Wizard of Oz study, 13 practicing analysts (Sec. 4), same scenario; JupyterLab extension; wizard aided by LLMs controls selection, quality, timing (Fig. 3) — contribution 1
- Findings -> design guidelines (Sec. 5, Sec. 6) — contribution 2
  - align intent/goals, varying assistance levels, understanding + engagement
  - context, timing, backgrounds matter
  - goal mismatch: speed/completion vs. methodical/robust planning
- Closing: more robust, reliable data analysis through richer assistants

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Doing data analysis means analysts have to make a lot of decisions about different tasks, for example data collection, data wrangling, statistical modeling and inference. For each choice there is analysis planning, where the analyst reasons about what the potential decisions will do by putting together their results, their prior experiences, and their domain and statistical knowledge. When the decisions are made, the focus moves to actually carrying out the choices with the right code and the right software tools, and we call this analysis execution. Then the analyst looks at the outcome of the execution and the process repeats again.

When analysis planning is inadequate this flow can get complicated, and analysts risk making arbitrary and ill-founded decisions, for lots of reasons. Analysts often have a hard time identifying and addressing the decision points that are relevant. They can focus too much on low-level details like tuning hyperparameters, or they miss high-level considerations such as alternative statistical or mental models. Often they center their execution decisions on workflows they are familiar with, even when approaches with other tools might be more applicable. Also, the flexibility in decision-making that nobody considers (and the biases that come with it) contributes to the reproducibility crisis in science. For example, when analysts get the same analysis task and the same dataset they often come to divergent conclusions.

Data analysis assistants try to bridge these gaps by helping analysts to execute and plan their analyses. Execution assistants based on AI (for example Copilot) help analysts implement their decisions (Fig. 1 A) by suggesting code or tools. Planning assistance is different, it may help analysts reason about their decisions (Fig. 1 B and C), articulate their hypotheses and mental models, and identify alternative decisions or rationales that they overlooked (Fig. 1). Considering alternatives systematically can deepen how well analysts understand the outcome variations that are latent to decision-making in data analysis. So planning assistance can be a transformative step towards analyses that are more principled, reliable and robust.

Large language models (LLMs) have improved capabilities for coding, language and generating visualizations, and this gives an opportunity to make planning and execution data analysis assistants a reality. Previous LLM-based assistants explored practical approaches for execution assistance, but planning is still unexplored (Fig. 2 bottom row).

You can't get effective planning suggestions just by feeding the current analysis context into an LLM, because it needs selective context, higher-level scaffolding, targeted prompts and sensitive triggers. Data analysis is iterative and it needs nuanced interpretation of prior results, statistics and domain knowledge to inform the next decisions, and execution-only assistants typically don't account for this (Fig. 2 A and B). Synthesizing these decisions may mean backtracking to a prior choice and deviating from the current approach (Fig. 1). Writing effective prompts can be difficult, and it can be hard to identify the right context to give so that the model does not cause hallucinatory analyses. Finally, data analysis is non-linear, it involves typing, reading and reflecting actions that are iterated and inter-woven, so the best timing for suggestions is less clear than it is in software engineering.

But essential questions about how to design planning assistants are still unanswered. In this work we explore the design of these AI-based assistants. We consider these research questions:

What types of specific planning assistance content could an assistant provide?

What data analysis suggestions do analysts find helpful and under what circumstances?

How do suggestions impact analysts’ workflows? To what extent do analysts prioritize their own ideas or adopt suggestions and explore alternative approaches?

To characterize the content of assistant suggestions (RQ 1), we did a literature review and we critically assessed data from a crowd-sourced analysis study, where 29 analyst teams analyzed the same dataset separately to answer the same research question (Sec. 3). We used these findings to develop categories of assistance content at different points in the end-to-end analysis process (Table 1).

To observe what analysts prefer (RQ2) and the effects (RQ3) of different suggestions, we ran a Wizard of Oz study with 13 practicing data analysts (Sec. 4), and this is our first contribution. We designed the study around the scenario from the crowd-sourced study that we looked at in the previous step. Participants worked through the same dataset and task and got suggestions from an experimenter behind the scenes who acted as a wizard. For the study we developed a JupyterLab extension which let the wizard surface suggestions to the participant while they used the notebook in a familiar way. This let the wizard (aided by LLMs) synthesize suggestions and manipulate the selection, quality and timing of recommendations (Fig. 3).

We synthesize what we found in the study (Sec. 5) into a set of design guidelines (Sec. 6), which is our second contribution. The guidelines are to align analysis intent and goals, support varying levels of suggestion assistance, and increase how much analysts understand and engage with the assistant's suggestions. We saw that the data analysis process can benefit from diverse forms of planning assistance, but only if the assistance context is carefully considered. Other factors, like the timing of suggestions or differences in the statistical and domain backgrounds of analysts, played a critical role in whether a suggestion was seen as helpful. Finally, we found that the goals of the analyst (i.e., speed and completion) and of planning assistance (i.e., methodical and robust planning) were different.

By characterizing how usable planning-equipped analysis assistants are, we want to make data analysis more robust and reliable by enabling assistants that are richer and more useful.

Analysts often struggle to identify and address relevant decision points [1,4]. They may overfocus on low-level details, such as tuning hyperparameters, or miss high-level considerations like alternative statistical or mental models [4]. They often center execution decisions on familiar workflows when approaches using other tools may be more applicable [4,5]. Further, unconsidered flexibility in decision-making (and the biases inherent in it) contributes to the scientific reproducibility crisis [6,7,8]. For instance, given the same analysis task and dataset, analysts often reach divergent conclusions [9,10,11,12,13,14,15].

Data analysis assistants seek to bridge these gaps by helping analysts execute and plan their analyses. AI-based execution assistants (such as Copilot [16]) help analysts implement decisions (Fig. 1 A) by suggesting code or tools. Planning assistance, by contrast, may help them reason about their decisions (Fig. 1 B and C), articulate hypotheses and mental models, and identify overlooked alternative decisions or rationales (Fig. 1). Systematically considering alternatives can deepen analysts’ understanding of the outcome variations latent to decision-making in data analysis [17,2,3]. Planning assistance can therefore be a transformative step towards more principled, reliable, and robust analyses.

The improved capabilities of large language models (LLMs) for coding, language, and visualization generation [18,19,20,21,22] offer an opportunity to make such planning and execution assistants a reality. Prior LLM-based assistants have explored practical approaches to execution assistance [23,24,25,26,27,28]; planning, however, remains unexplored (Fig. 2 bottom row).

Effective planning suggestions cannot be achieved simply by feeding the current analysis context into an LLM, as this requires selective context, higher-level scaffolding, targeted prompts, and sensitive triggers. The iterative nature of data analysis demands nuanced interpretation of prior results, statistics, and domain knowledge to inform subsequent decisions [29,30,5,31], which execution-only assistants typically do not account for (Fig. 2 A and B). Synthesizing such decisions may require backtracking to a prior choice and deviating from the current approach (Fig. 1). Authoring effective prompts can be difficult [32,33], and the right context to provide so as not to cause hallucinatory analyses [34] may be hard to identify. Finally, data analysis is a non-linear activity involving iterated and inter-woven actions of typing, reading, and reflecting, which makes the optimal timing of suggestions less clear than in software engineering.

Essential questions about the design of planning assistants thus remain unanswered. In this work, we explore the design of such AI-based assistants, considering the following research questions:

What types of specific planning assistance content could an assistant provide?

What data analysis suggestions do analysts find helpful and under what circumstances?

How do suggestions impact analysts’ workflows? To what extent do analysts prioritize their own ideas or adopt suggestions and explore alternative approaches?

To characterize assistant suggestion content (RQ 1), we conducted a literature review and critically assessed data from a crowd-sourced analysis study [9], in which 29 analyst teams separately analyzed the same dataset to answer the same research question (Sec. 3). From these findings we developed categories of assistance content across points in the end-to-end analysis process (Table 1).

To observe analysts’ preferences for (RQ2) and the effects of (RQ3) different suggestions, we conducted a Wizard of Oz study with 13 practicing data analysts (Sec. 4), our first contribution. We designed the study around the scenario of the crowd-sourced study [9] examined in the previous step. Participants worked through the same dataset and task while receiving suggestions from an experimenter acting as a wizard behind the scenes. To facilitate the study, we developed a JupyterLab extension that let the wizard surface suggestions to the participant as they used the notebook in a familiar manner. This allowed the wizard (aided by LLMs) to synthesize suggestions and manipulate the selection, quality, and timing of recommendations (Fig. 3).

As our second contribution, we synthesize the findings of our study (Sec. 5) into a set of design guidelines (Sec. 6) to align analysis intent and goals, support varying levels of suggestion assistance, and increase analysts’ understanding of and engagement with the assistant’s suggestions. We observed that the data analysis process can benefit from diverse forms of planning assistance, but only when the assistance context is carefully considered. Additional factors, such as the timing of suggestions or variations in analysts’ statistical and domain backgrounds, played a critical role in how helpful a suggestion was perceived to be. Finally, we found differences in goals between the analyst (i.e., speed and completion) and planning assistance (i.e., methodical and robust planning).

By characterizing the usability of planning-equipped analysis assistants, we aim to make data analysis more robust and reliable through richer and more useful assistants.
